title: Sequences and Basic Series Convergence Tests

questions.q: Determine whether the sequence $a_n=\frac{3n+1}{n}$ converges, and if so, find its limit.
Determine whether the sequence $a_n=(-1)^n$ converges.
questions.answer: The sequence oscillates between $-1$ and $1$ and never settles on a single value, so it diverges.

questions.q: Determine whether $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}3\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$ converges, and if so, find its sum.
Determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^n$ converges.
Use the $n$th-term test to show $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n}{n+1}$ diverges.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n}{n+1}=1\neq0$. Since the terms don't approach $0$, the series diverges by the $n$th-term test.

questions.q: Use the Integral Test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^2}$ converges.
questions.answer: Let $f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2}$, positive, continuous, decreasing for $x\geq1$. $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx=\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_1^{\infty}=0-(-1)=1$, a finite value. By the Integral Test, the series converges.

questions.q: Use the Integral Test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}$ converges (the harmonic series).
questions.answer: $\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x}\,dx=\left[\ln x\right]_1^{\infty}=\infty$. Diverges. So the harmonic series diverges by the Integral Test.

sections.heading: The comparison and limit comparison tests

questions.q: Use the Direct Comparison Test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^2+1}$ converges, comparing to $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$.
questions.answer: $\frac{1}{n^2+1}<\frac{1}{n^2}$ for all $n\geq1$, and $\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$ converges (p-series with $p=2>1$). By Direct Comparison, $\sum\frac{1}{n^2+1}$ converges.

questions.q: Use the Limit Comparison Test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{2n}{n^2+3}$ converges, comparing to $\sum\frac{1}{n}$.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2n/(n^2+3)}{1/n}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2n^2}{n^2+3}=2$, a finite positive value. Since $\sum\frac{1}{n}$ diverges (harmonic), $\sum\frac{2n}{n^2+3}$ also diverges by the Limit Comparison Test.

questions.q: Plot the first 6 terms of $a_n=\frac{3n+1}{n}$ (from the earlier question) and describe how the points behave as $n$ increases.
questions.answer: $a_1=4$, $a_2=3.5$, $a_3\approx3.33$, $a_4=3.25$, $a_5=3.2$, $a_6\approx3.17$. The points decrease and cluster tighter and tighter around the horizontal line $y=3$, visually confirming the limit found algebraically.

questions.q: Determine whether $a_n=\frac{n}{n+1}$ is monotonic (always increasing or always decreasing), and find an upper bound.
questions.answer: $a_{n+1}-a_n=\frac{n+1}{n+2}-\frac{n}{n+1}=\frac{(n+1)^2-n(n+2)}{(n+1)(n+2)}=\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}>0$, so the sequence is strictly increasing. Since $a_n=1-\frac{1}{n+1}<1$ for all $n$, it is bounded above by $1$.

questions.q: State the Monotonic Sequence Theorem, and use it to conclude that $a_n=\frac{n}{n+1}$ converges.
questions.answer: The Monotonic Sequence Theorem states that every bounded, monotonic sequence converges. Since $a_n=\frac{n}{n+1}$ is increasing and bounded above by $1$ (shown above), it must converge (in fact to $1$).

questions.q: State the p-series test for $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^p}$, and classify convergence for $p=1$, $p=\frac{3}{2}$, and $p=\frac{1}{2}$.
questions.answer: $\sum\frac{1}{n^p}$ converges if $p>1$ and diverges if $p\leq1$. $p=1$: diverges (harmonic). $p=\frac{3}{2}>1$: converges. $p=\frac{1}{2}\leq1$: diverges.

questions.q: Use the p-series test (after simplifying) to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{5}{n^{0.9}}$ converges.
questions.answer: This is $5\sum\frac{1}{n^{0.9}}$, a constant multiple of a p-series with $p=0.9\leq1$. Diverges.

sections.heading: Series review: choosing the right test

questions.q: For each series, name the most efficient test to apply (do not fully evaluate):
A sequence is defined recursively by $a_1=2$, $a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n+6}{2}$. Compute $a_2$, $a_3$, and $a_4$, and conjecture the limit if the sequence converges.
questions.answer: $a_2=\frac{2+6}{2}=4$. $a_3=\frac{4+6}{2}=5$. $a_4=\frac{5+6}{2}=5.5$. The terms appear to approach $6$ (if $L=\frac{L+6}{2}$, then $2L=L+6 \Rightarrow L=6$).

questions.q: Verify that if a recursively defined sequence $a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n+6}{2}$ converges to a limit $L$, then $L$ must satisfy $L=6$.
questions.answer: If $a_n\to L$, then $a_{n+1}\to L$ as well, so taking the limit of both sides: $L=\frac{L+6}{2} \Rightarrow 2L=L+6 \Rightarrow L=6$, confirming the conjecture.

questions.q: Find the sum of $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n$ (note the series starts at $n=2$, not $n=0$).
questions.answer: Using $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r^n=\frac{1}{1-r}$ and subtracting the first two terms ($n=0,1$): $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n=\frac{1}{1-2/3}-1-\frac{2}{3}=3-\frac{5}{3}=\frac{4}{3}$.

questions.q: Express the repeating decimal $0.\overline{45}$ as a geometric series and find its exact fractional value.
Evaluate the telescoping series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)$ by examining its partial sums.
questions.answer: $S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)=1-\frac{1}{N+1}$ (all middle terms cancel). As $N\to\infty$: $S_N\to1-0=1$. The series converges to $1$.
